name: Boosts
description: Interventions that build people's own decision-making competences or agency, as opposed to nudges that steer behaviour directly. Examples include simple decision aids and training in how to read risk information.
design_relevance_note: A design alternative to nudging: teach or equip users to decide for themselves (for example clearer risk formats, inoculation messages) rather than steering them.
myth_risk_note: Presented as an evidence-based alternative to nudging, but the evidence for boosts as a class is conceptual so far.
prevalence_note: Discussed in policy and behavioural-public-policy circles; rarely implemented by name.

findings.description: Boosts and nudges are conceptually distinct classes of behavioral policy intervention, not two labels for the same thing: they differ in immediate intervention target (boosts target competence/decision-making tools; nudges target behavior directly), theoretical roots (boosts draw on the 'simple heuristics' / ecological-rationality research program; nudges draw on the heuristics-and-biases program), causal pathway (boosts work through changing a person's repertoire of skills/knowledge/decision tools; nudges work by exploiting existing cognitive biases or default psychological responses), assumed cognitive architecture, reversibility of effects once the intervention is withdrawn (boost effects are argued to persist; nudge effects are argued to typically require the nudge to remain in place), programmatic ambition, and normative/autonomy implications.
findings.source_title: Nudging and Boosting: Steering or Empowering Good Decisions

findings.description: Distinguishing nudges, technocognition and boosts, the authors map boosts for digital environments into two groups: those enhancing people's agency (e.g. self-nudging, deliberate ignorance) and those boosting competences of reasoning and resilience to manipulation (e.g. simple decision aids, inoculation). A conceptual map, not an effect-size estimate.
findings.source_title: Citizens Versus the Internet: Confronting Digital Challenges With Cognitive Tools
findings.source_venue: Psychological Science in the Public Interest
